opus-5.5.text:
I think there are a few bottlenecks, and they're quite different from the ones we faced with traditional physics simulators.

The first, and probably the biggest, is physical consistency. Video generation models have become remarkably good at producing things that *look* right. But looking right and being physically right are not the same. When you use a video model as a simulator for robotics, you care a lot about contact: whether the gripper actually grasps the object, whether the object slips, whether the force is enough to push something across the table. Today's models often get the visual appearance plausible but violate object permanence, mass conservation, or rigid-body constraints. An object might deform when it shouldn't, or a cup passes slightly through a hand. For a human viewer that's a small glitch. For a robot policy being trained or evaluated in that world, it's a huge problem, because the policy will learn to exploit those errors.

The second bottleneck is action controllability. In a classical simulator, you send a joint torque or a target position and the simulator tells you exactly what happens. With a video model, the conditioning on actions is still relatively weak. Many models are trained mostly on internet video, where there are no action labels at all. So getting the model to respond precisely and faithfully to fine-grained robot actions, rather than just generating a "reasonable-looking" continuation, is still hard. And you need that precision if you want to do closed-loop policy evaluation or reinforcement learning inside the model.

Third is long-horizon stability. Errors accumulate. If you roll out for a few seconds, things look fine, but over tens of seconds or minutes the scene drifts, objects change identity, the background changes. Robotics tasks are often long-horizon, so this compounding error really limits how useful the model is as a simulator.

And then there's the practical side: speed and cost. A traditional physics engine can run thousands of times faster than real time on parallel hardware. Video models are expensive to run, often slower than real time. If you want to do large-scale RL, where you need billions of interaction steps, that's a serious constraint.

Finally, I'd mention evaluation itself. We don't yet have good metrics to tell us how faithful a world model is as a simulator. Visual quality metrics like FVD don't really capture whether the physics is correct, or whether a policy's success rate in the world model correlates with its success rate in the real world. That correlation is ultimately what we care about.

That said, I'm quite optimistic. The thing video models offer that classical simulators never could is breadth: you don't need to hand-build every asset, every material, every deformable object. The long tail of the real world is exactly where traditional simulation breaks down. So I think the future is probably some combination: using the strengths of learned world models for diversity and realism, while grounding them with more physical structure, more robot interaction data, and better action conditioning. Closing those gaps is one of the most exciting problems in robotics right now.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. The way I think about it, the bottleneck isn't really visual fidelity anymore. The videos look great. The bottleneck is whether the model actually respects physics, and whether you can interact with it the way you interact with a real simulator.

Let me unpack that a bit. When we use a simulator like MuJoCo or Isaac Gym for robot learning, we care about a few things. The dynamics have to be consistent. If I push on an object with a certain force, it should move in a predictable way, and the same action from the same state should produce roughly the same outcome. Video generation models today are trained to produce plausible-looking frames, not physically correct ones. So you get objects that pass through each other, contacts that don't produce the right reaction, a cup that sort of floats for a frame before it lands. For a human watching, that's a minor artifact. For a policy that's learning from those rollouts, it's a false signal about how the world works, and the policy will exploit it.

The second piece is action conditioning. A simulator takes a state and an action and gives you the next state. Most video models were built the other way around, from text or an image to a clip. Getting them to respond faithfully to a low-level robot action, joint torques or end-effector commands, is still hard. The action signal is weak compared to the visual prior the model has absorbed, so the model tends to generate what usually happens in videos like this rather than what this specific action would cause.

Then there's long-horizon consistency. Errors compound. A rollout that drifts after two seconds is fine for a demo but useless for learning a task that takes thirty seconds. And finally cost. A physics simulator can give you tens of thousands of environment steps per second on one GPU. A video model gives you a handful of frames per second, if you're lucky. Reinforcement learning is sample hungry, so that gap matters a lot.

So if I had to put it in one sentence: the models have learned what the world looks like, but not yet how the world responds. Closing that gap, with better action grounding, some kind of physical structure or verification in the loop, and much faster inference, is where I think the real work is right now.

astra-6.text:
I think the main bottleneck is that generating a video that looks realistic is different from generating a simulation that behaves correctly. For simulation, you need to take an action and see its consequences. If a robot pushes an object, how does that object move? Does it respond consistently to the force, the friction, and the contact?

A video model might produce something visually convincing without getting those interactions right. And that matters if you use it to train a policy, because the policy may learn to exploit mistakes in the model instead of learning behavior that works in the real world.

So I would focus on action conditioning and physical consistency, especially over long sequences. Visual quality is useful, but the key question is whether the model can reliably predict what happens when an agent acts.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the biggest bottleneck is physical consistency. Video generation models can produce something that looks realistic, but looking realistic is different from behaving like a reliable simulator. For simulation, if a robot takes an action, we need the model to predict the consequences of that action accurately, and to keep doing that over a long sequence.

For example, if the robot pushes an object, the object should move consistently with its geometry, contact, and friction. A visually plausible video can still get those interactions wrong. And if we train a policy in that environment, it may learn to exploit those mistakes instead of learning something that works in the real world.

So I would focus on action conditioning, physical consistency, and long-horizon prediction. The question is whether these models can reliably tell us what will happen when an agent intervenes in the world.
